client: I've been really struggling ever since my grandfather passed away a few weeks ago, and with my final exams starting next week, I just can't seem to focus on anything. Every time I sit down to study, I end up staring at the wall or thinking about him, and then I feel this wave of guilt like I'm failing him by not doing well. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help me actually get through these exams, but I didn't know what else to do.
therapist: What you're carrying right now is genuinely heavy — grief and high-stakes pressure arriving at the same time is an incredibly difficult combination, and it makes complete sense that your mind keeps drifting to your grandfather rather than your notes. I also want to gently notice that thought you mentioned — that not doing well on exams means you're *failing him* — because that's a really painful belief worth exploring together. What do you think your grandfather would actually say if he knew you were grieving him while trying to study for your exams?

client: Honestly, I know logically he would probably tell me not to worry about the exams and just take care of myself. He was always really gentle like that, never put pressure on me about grades or anything. But knowing what he'd say and actually believing it are two completely different things, because the guilt doesn't really care about logic right now.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you can already hear his voice so clearly — that gentleness he showed you is still with you, even if grief is making it hard to feel it right now. You've touched on something that's at the heart of a lot of CBT work: knowing something intellectually and *feeling* it as true are genuinely different experiences, and that gap isn't a failure of logic on your part — it's just how grief works. I'm curious, when that wave of guilt hits while you're trying to study, what does the thought actually sound like in your head — is it more like a specific voice or accusation, or more like a heavy feeling without clear words?

client: It's more like a specific accusation, actually — it sounds like "you should be studying right now, and the fact that you can't even do that means you're going to let everyone down." It's not even really about him specifically, it's more like his death kind of unlocked this fear that I'm fundamentally not capable of handling things when it matters most. That's the part that scares me more than the exams themselves, honestly.
therapist: That's a really important insight — you've just uncovered something much deeper than exam stress, which takes courage to look at directly. That core fear, "I'm fundamentally not capable when it matters," is what we'd call a core belief in CBT, and it's worth noticing that *recognizing you can't focus while grieving* is actually very different evidence from *being incapable* — one is a very human response to loss, the other is a story about who you are. What would you say to a close friend who lost someone they loved and then struggled to concentrate a few weeks later — would that feel like proof to you that *they* couldn't handle things?

client: No, obviously I wouldn't think that about a friend — I'd probably tell them to be easy on themselves and that it makes total sense they're struggling. But when you put it that way, I almost feel like I'm being tricked into being kinder to myself, like my brain is waiting to catch the loophole that makes my situation different and actually as bad as it feels. I guess I just don't fully trust that applying that same logic to myself will actually stick when I'm sitting alone at my desk at midnight trying to get through a practice exam.
therapist: That instinct your brain has — hunting for the loophole that makes your situation the exception — is actually one of the most common and sneaky ways self-criticism keeps itself alive, and the fact that you can *see* it doing that is genuinely a sign of real self-awareness, not a trick. You're right that insight in a conversation doesn't automatically translate to 2am at your desk, which is why it helps to have something concrete to reach for in that moment rather than relying on willpower alone. If we could design a small, specific thing you could do or say to yourself when that midnight guilt hits — something that feels honest rather than like a hollow pep talk — what do you think might actually have a chance of landing for you?

client: I've been trying to think about that and the honest answer is I'm not sure anything will feel true enough in that moment to actually cut through it. Maybe something like reminding myself that my grandfather knew who I was before these exams and that doesn't change based on how I perform — but even saying that out loud now, part of me is already worried it'll just feel like words on a page when I'm exhausted and panicking at midnight. I guess I'm skeptical that I can manufacture the right phrase in advance when the feeling itself is so much bigger than any sentence I could come up with.
therapist: Your skepticism is actually really honest and worth respecting — you're not going to trick yourself out of a feeling that big with a single sentence, and pretending otherwise would feel hollow. What you said about your grandfather knowing who you were *before* the exams is genuinely meaningful though, and rather than it being a phrase you recite, I wonder if it could be more like a small ritual — maybe even glancing at a photo of him, or taking 60 seconds to just *miss him* instead of fighting the feeling — so that instead of trying to think your way past the grief, you briefly make room for it and then return to the page. Does that kind of approach — working *with* the feeling rather than against it — feel any more believable to you than trying to find the perfect words?

client: That actually does feel slightly more believable, yeah — like I'm not trying to pretend the grief isn't there but also not just drowning in it. I do have a photo of him on my phone and I think there's something that feels more honest about just letting myself be sad for a minute instead of trying to logic my way out of it. My worry is that 60 seconds turns into an hour and then I've completely lost the study session, but I can see that's probably my anxiety talking more than a realistic prediction.
therapist: It's really encouraging that something finally feels a little more honest and workable — and you've already done something important just now by catching your own anxiety making a catastrophic prediction and naming it for what it is. You could even experiment with making the boundary concrete — setting a two-minute timer when you look at his photo, which gives the grief real permission to exist without the fear of it taking over completely. How do you feel about trying that small ritual once before your exams start, just to see what it's actually like rather than letting your anxiety write the story of how it'll go?

client: I think I'm willing to try it, though I'm a little nervous about what might come up when I actually let myself sit with the grief instead of constantly pushing it away. The timer idea helps actually, because it gives it a shape — like there's a container for it rather than just an open door I'm afraid to walk through. I just hope I don't do it once and then decide it didn't work and use that as proof that nothing will help me get through this.
therapist: There's something really hopeful in how you just framed that — you've moved from "nothing will feel true enough" to "I'm willing to try," which is a meaningful shift even if it doesn't feel dramatic. I also want to gently flag the trap you just named: going in with the expectation that it has to "work" the first time is actually a way anxiety sneaks back in and sets you up to confirm the belief that nothing helps — so the goal for the first try isn't for it to fix anything, just to notice what happens. What would "it worked well enough to try again" look like for you, rather than "it worked" in some complete way?

client: I think "worked well enough to try again" would mean that after the two minutes, I was able to actually return to studying instead of either spiraling further or feeling completely numb and disconnected. It doesn't have to feel healing or meaningful in some big way — just that I got through it and came back to the page without feeling worse than before. That actually feels like a bar I could realistically clear, which is different from how I've been thinking about it.
therapist: That's a really grounded and compassionate bar to set for yourself — and notice how different it feels from the "fundamentally not capable" story you walked in with today. You've moved from needing to prove something to simply asking: *can I return to the page?* — which is a much kinder and more honest measure of getting through a hard moment. As you head into this week, what feels like the most important thing to hold onto from what we've talked about today?

client: I think the most important thing is probably that the grief and the struggling to focus aren't proof of something being fundamentally wrong with me — they're just what happens when something this painful lands at the worst possible time. I didn't expect to feel even slightly less tangled up about it coming in here today, so that's something. I'm still scared about the exams, but it feels a little less like I'm fighting on two fronts at once now.
therapist: What you just said is really worth holding onto — that reframe, that struggle during grief is *human timing* rather than evidence of a fundamental flaw, is something you arrived at yourself today, which means it has a much better chance of being there when you need it. It makes sense that there's still some fear underneath — you're not through it yet — but you came in feeling tangled and you're leaving with a small, honest plan and a slightly quieter inner critic, and that's real progress. Be gentle with yourself this week, and I hope you'll let your grandfather's gentleness toward you be something you borrow for yourself when midnight comes.

client: That last part actually got to me a little — "borrow his gentleness for yourself" is a way of putting it I hadn't thought of before, and it feels less like a therapy technique and more like something real. I think I'm going to try the ritual tonight actually, before the exams even start, just to see what it's like when the pressure isn't at its peak. I'm still not sure I fully trust that I can hold onto any of this when things get hard, but I think that's just something I have to find out rather than decide in advance.
therapist: There's something quietly courageous in what you just said — choosing to try the ritual tonight, on your own terms, before the pressure peaks, is exactly the kind of gentle self-trust you've been building toward in this conversation. And that last part — "something I have to find out rather than decide in advance" — is honestly one of the most important shifts a person can make, because it trades the exhausting work of predicting and controlling for the simpler, braver act of just showing up and seeing. I think your grandfather would recognize that in you.
